B.1: Six thousand dollars. That is the size of a new tax deduction for people over sixty-five, and it runs through twenty twenty-eight. But the I R S rules say some seniors get all of it, some get only part, and some get nothing at all. In the next few minutes you will see exactly which one you are, and what this deduction is really worth in dollars. Every number comes from the I R S itself, and I will show you the one line most people forget to fill in.
B.2: Meet three people. Dolores is sixty-seven and single, and she lives on Social Security plus an I R A. Tom is seventy and retired, and his wife Ruth is sixty-two and still works. And Hank is sixty-eight, with a big pension and a big I R A. Three people, three very different results. Dolores wants to know how much tax she pays. Tom and Ruth want to know what they can claim. Hank wants to know why his deduction is so small. Keep an eye on Ruth, because her story has a surprise.
B.3: All the numbers in this video come from the Internal Revenue Service: Publication five fifty-four, the Tax Guide for Seniors, the Schedule one A form, Publication nine fifteen on Social Security taxes, and the I R S inflation rules for twenty twenty-six. Nothing here comes from the news. Every example uses the exact steps printed on the I R S forms. Let's start with what the deduction actually is.
B.4: Part one: the deduction. Starting in twenty twenty-five and running through twenty twenty-eight, anyone age sixty-five or older can take an extra deduction of six thousand dollars. A married couple where both spouses qualify can take twelve thousand. The I R S counts you as sixty-five on the day before your birthday, so what matters is reaching sixty-five by the last day of the tax year. It works whether you take the standard deduction or itemize.
B.5: You claim it on Schedule one A, Part five, of your Form ten forty. It does not come automatically. The I R S does not apply it for you, and a Social Security check does not include it. Ask your tax preparer for it by its official name: the enhanced deduction for seniors. If you file your own return, or use a free helper, you need to make sure that box is filled in. Now let's stack the numbers for twenty twenty-six.
B.6: A single person gets a standard deduction of sixteen thousand one hundred dollars. Because Dolores is over sixty-five, add two thousand fifty dollars more. Then add the new six thousand dollars. That is twenty-four thousand one hundred fifty dollars of income that Dolores does not pay federal income tax on, before she pays a cent. Write that number down, because everything else builds on it.
B.7: For a married couple filing jointly, the standard deduction is thirty-two thousand two hundred dollars. If both spouses are sixty-five or older, add sixteen hundred fifty dollars each, and six thousand dollars each. That brings the total to forty-seven thousand five hundred dollars. If only one spouse is over sixty-five, only that spouse's extra amounts count. For many couples living mostly on Social Security, this can mean no federal income tax at all.
B.8: But here is the part everybody gets wrong. A deduction is not a six thousand dollar check. It lowers the income you are taxed on, so what it saves depends on your tax bracket. In the twelve percent bracket, six thousand dollars saves seven hundred twenty dollars. In the twenty-two percent bracket, it saves thirteen hundred twenty. Real money, but not six thousand. Many videos say you save six thousand dollars. That is not what the form does.
B.9: Let's see it with Dolores. She gets twenty-four thousand dollars a year from Social Security and takes thirty thousand from her I R A. Using the I R S worksheet, eleven thousand three hundred dollars of her Social Security is taxable. Her income on the return is forty-one thousand three hundred. After her twenty-four thousand one hundred fifty dollar deduction, she is taxed on seventeen thousand one hundred fifty.
B.10: Her federal income tax comes to eighteen hundred ten dollars. Without the new six thousand dollar deduction, it would have been twenty-five hundred thirty. That is seven hundred twenty dollars saved every year, from one line on one form. And notice that part of her Social Security is still taxed. This deduction does not make your benefits tax free. Your own result depends on your bracket and your income, so run your own numbers.
B.11: If Social Security is your only income, there is a good chance you pay nothing on it. Take a single person with thirty thousand dollars in benefits. The I R S counts half, fifteen thousand dollars, which is far below the twenty-five thousand dollar line, so none of the benefits are taxable. The taxes come when you add an I R A, a pension, interest, or work income on top of the benefits.
B.12: Here is how the tax on Social Security works. The I R S adds half of your benefits to your other income. If that total is above twenty-five thousand dollars for a single person, or thirty-two thousand for a married couple filing jointly, part of your benefits becomes taxable. Above thirty-four thousand, or forty-four thousand for couples, up to eighty-five percent can be taxable. Never more than eighty-five.
B.13: Now, who loses part of it. The deduction shrinks when your income goes above seventy-five thousand dollars, or one hundred fifty thousand for joint filers. The Schedule one A takes six percent of every dollar above that line off your six thousand. For a single person, the deduction is completely gone at one hundred seventy-five thousand. For a couple, it is gone at two hundred fifty thousand.
B.14: Look at Hank. His income is one hundred forty thousand dollars, which is sixty-five thousand over the line. Six percent of sixty-five thousand is thirty-nine hundred dollars, so his deduction is six thousand minus thirty-nine hundred: twenty-one hundred dollars. And here is the trap: every extra thousand dollars he takes out of his I R A costs him sixty dollars of this deduction. If Hank had taken twenty thousand dollars less, he would have kept twelve hundred more.
B.15: Now, who gets nothing. If you are married, you must file jointly, so married filing separately gets no senior deduction. Each person needs a valid Social Security number, issued before the due date of the return. And the age test is for each person. Tom is seventy, but Ruth is only sixty-two. So Tom claims six thousand dollars, and Ruth claims nothing until she reaches sixty-five.
B.16: So what should you do this year? One: before December thirty-first, check your income. If you are close to seventy-five or one hundred fifty thousand dollars, an I R A withdrawal or a Roth conversion can cost you part of this deduction. Two: if you have a pension or an I R A, review your withholding with Form W four P, so April has no surprise. Three: ask for free help.
B.17: There is one more tool. You can choose to have federal income tax withheld from your Social Security check, by filling out Form W four V. If you do not, the I R S says you may have to request more withholding from other income, or pay estimated tax during the year. The deduction lowers your bill, but you still want the bill to be paid evenly, not in one big payment in April.
B.18: For free help, the I R S runs Volunteer Income Tax Assistance and Tax Counseling for the Elderly, with trained volunteers at sites near you. And remember the clock: this deduction is written into the law for twenty twenty-five through twenty twenty-eight. For those years, check it every single time you file. It is easy to miss, and it is worth hundreds of dollars.
B.19: To recap. One: six thousand dollars per person, age sixty-five or older. Two: it stacks on top of your standard deduction. Three: it saves your tax bracket times six thousand, not six thousand. Four: it shrinks by six percent above seventy-five or one hundred fifty thousand. Five: you need joint filing, a Social Security number, and age sixty-five for each person.
